# The Harms of Frequent Medical Screening: Overdiagnosis, Anxiety, and the Case for Evidence-Based Intervals

**A Research Perspective**

---

## 1. Introduction

Population screening programs rest on an intuitive premise: finding disease early must be better than finding it late. However, four decades of epidemiological research have complicated this assumption. Screening is a form of testing applied to *asymptomatic* populations, and it must therefore satisfy a stricter evidentiary standard than diagnostic testing. This report examines the principal harms of frequent screening—overdiagnosis, false positives, patient anxiety, and downstream overtreatment—and models how these might manifest in a hypothetical annual screening program.

The framework for evaluation remains that of Wilson and Jungner (1968), commissioned by the WHO, which requires that screening be offered only when the condition is an important health problem, the natural history is understood, an early detectable stage exists, and treatment at that stage is more effective than treatment after symptoms appear. Many current practices fail to meet these criteria at annual frequency.

---

## 2. Overdiagnosis: Definition and Magnitude

### 2.1 Conceptual Basis

Overdiagnosis is the detection of a condition that would never have caused symptoms or death in the patient's lifetime. It is not an error in diagnosis—the finding is real—but an error in *prognostication at the population level*. Its fundamental driver is length-time and lead-time bias: screening preferentially identifies slow-growing, indolent disease, because fast-growing disease presents symptomatically between screening intervals.

Because indolent and aggressive disease cannot reliably be distinguished at detection, overdiagnosis converts directly into overtreatment.

### 2.2 Quantitative Evidence

**Prostate cancer.** Welch and Albertsen (2009, *JNCI*) estimated that, in the PSA era, over 1 million US men were diagnosed with prostate cancer who would otherwise never have been diagnosed; approximately 1 in 5 men diagnosed through screening had cancer that would never have become clinically apparent—a figure other analyses place as high as 42–56%. The PLCO trial (Andriole et al., 2009, *NEJM*) found no prostate cancer mortality benefit from annual PSA screening combined with DRE over 13 years of follow-up. The ERSPC trial (Schröder et al., 2012, *Lancet*) found a benefit but with a substantial number needed to invite for screening: approximately **1 prostate cancer death averted per ~1,000 men screened over ~11 years**, against a much larger number of men diagnosed and treated.

**Breast cancer.** Estimates of overdiagnosis from mammography range from ~10% to ~30% of screen-detected cancers (Marmot et al., 2012, *Lancet*, independent UK Panel; Jørgensen & Gøtzsche, 2009, *BMJ*). The UK Panel concluded that for every breast cancer death prevented, approximately **three women were overdiagnosed and treated unnecessarily**. DCIS, nearly all of which is screen-detected, illustrates the uncertainty: contemporary data suggest low breast cancer mortality in DCIS patients regardless of treatment intensity, prompting the ongoing COMET trial (Comprehensive Cohort study) of active monitoring versus standard treatment.

**Thyroid cancer (South Korea).** This represents the most complete natural experiment in the overdiagnosis literature. After neck ultrasound was added to a national health checkup program in 1999, thyroid cancer incidence rose ~15-fold (Ahn et al., 2014, *NEJM*; Ahn et al., 2016, *NEJM*), while mortality remained flat—implying that roughly 99% of the additional diagnoses were overdiagnosed. Survey data suggested approximately one-third of Korean adults had undergone opportunistic thyroid screening. Padberg and colleagues' broader reviews confirm that subclinical papillary microcarcinoma is present in a substantial fraction of the general population at autopsy.

**Lung nodules.** The National Lung Screening Trial (NLST; Aberle et al., 2011, *NEJM*) documented a 20% lung-cancer-specific mortality benefit from low-dose CT in high-risk smokers—but also a **96.4% false-positive rate** among positive screens, when judged against clinically significant endpoints.

### 2.3 Key Analytical Point

A consistent signature of overdiagnosis is the **incidence–mortality dissociation**: incidence rises steeply after a screening program begins while mortality is unchanged. Where this pattern is observed—thyroid cancer in Korea, testicular "microtumors," small renal masses, DCIS—clinicians should infer that a meaningful share of detected lesions are clinically irrelevant.

---

## 3. False Positives and the Cascade of Follow-Up Care

Screening tests applied to low-prevalence populations suffer mathematically from poor positive predictive value, regardless of reasonable sensitivity and specificity. If a condition has a prevalence of 0.5% and a test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity, more than **90% of positive results are false**.

Documented consequences:

- **NLST**: 39% of participants experienced at least one false-positive abnormality over three annual rounds; ~2.5% underwent an invasive procedure (biopsy or surgery), some with serious complications (a reported mortality of ~2 per 100 invasive procedures with benign findings).
- **Ovarian cancer screening**: The PLCO trial (Buys et al., 2011, *JAMA*) and the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (Jacobs et al., 2016, *JAMA*) found no mortality benefit; a majority of women with false-positive results underwent surgical intervention (oophorectomy), with reported serious surgical complication rates in the range of ~3–15% in screened populations.
- **Routine ECG/stress testing in asymptomatic adults**: The USPSTF (I and D recommendations, 2018) specifically cites the cascade from false positives to invasive coronary angiography, with associated risks of contrast nephropathy, bleeding, arrhythmia, and radiation exposure, as the basis for recommending *against* such screening.

---

## 4. Patient Anxiety and Psychological Harms

Psychological harm is the least quantified but most pervasive outcome. Relevant findings:

- **"Abnormal" labels persist.** Brodersen and colleagues developed the *Consequences of Screening in Breast Cancer* (COS-BC) questionnaire and demonstrated in the Danish mammography program that women with false-positive results had measured psychosocial harm—elevated anxiety, sleep disturbance, and negative effects on sexuality and daily life—**persisting up to three years after cancer was excluded** (Brodersen & Siersma, 2013, *Annals of Family Medicine*).
- **Immediate effects are near-universal.** Surveys around screening mammography consistently find that a large majority of women recalled for further imaging report anxiety at recall, with a substantial minority reporting it "as bad as or worse than" they imagined cancer would be.
- **Cascade anxiety in lung screening.** NLST follow-up studies documented distress in the substantial group of participants undergoing nodule surveillance, compounded over repeated annual rounds of indeterminate findings.
- **The labeling effect.** Being converted from a "healthy person" to a "patient" carries measurable effects: studies of incidentally found hypertension and of the prediabetes label show altered self-perception, increased sick-day behavior, and reduced workplace participation in some cohorts. McCormack and colleagues' work on "the burden of being labeled" is representative of this literature.
- **The "unquantified counterfactual" problem.** Jørgensen and Gøtzsche (2009) showed that informational materials for screening programs (in multiple countries) systematically overstated benefits and omitted overdiagnosis—meaning even the *consent* process underestimates harms, which itself is an ethical and psychological injury.

---

## 5. A Hypothetical Population Analysis: Modeling an Annual Screening Program

**Setup:** A hypothetical cohort of 100,000 adults aged 50–70 is screened annually for a slow-progressing neoplasm with lifetime penetrance of clinically significant disease ~2%. The screening test has 90% sensitivity, 95% specificity.
